Insinuate

in-SIN-yoo-ayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To insinuate is to suggest or hint at something, usually unpleasant, without stating it directly.

The email didn't accuse anyone by name, but it clearly insinuated that someone on the team had leaked the report.

Worked Example

The critic's review never said the restaurant was unsanitary, but it insinuated as much by mentioning the health inspector's visit three separate times.

Insinuate is about implying something negative indirectly -- letting the audience draw the ugly conclusion themselves.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

imply: To imply is to let words or evidence carry an unstated conclusion of any kind -- good, bad, or neutral; a rising sales chart implies growth. To insinuate is narrower and darker: a person deliberately plants an unflattering idea while never owning it. Anything can imply; it takes a motive to insinuate.

suggest: To suggest is to point toward an idea indirectly, and the word is wholly neutral -- data can suggest a trend, a friend can suggest a film. Insinuate is never neutral: it hints slyly at something damaging or unflattering. Everything from weather to numbers can suggest; to insinuate takes intent and a target.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

state: to say something directly and plainly

declare: to announce something clearly and openly

Where it sits · how openly the charge is made — hint → insinuate → allege

hint vs. insinuate: A hint is lighter than an insinuation: a gentle hint might be no more than a raised eyebrow or a knowing smile, easy to miss and easy to deny, while to insinuate is to steer an audience deliberately toward one specific unpleasant conclusion.

allege vs. insinuate: To allege goes further than to insinuate: an insinuation never states the charge outright, while to allege is to put the accusation into open words -- plainly made, even if not yet proven.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: into (Latin in-)

root — sinu-

root — sinu-: curve, fold, bay (Latin sinus)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or perform an action (Latin -atus)

Put it together

Put it together: Insinuate comes from Latin in- ("into") + sinus ("a curve or fold") -- literally to work your way into something along a winding path, the way an indirect hint slips into a conversation without a direct approach.

Use the root in a new word: sinuous

Use the root in a new word: sinuous: The river took a sinuous path through the valley, curving back on itself again and again.

Word Choice

Insinuate almost always carries a negative undertone -- it's for hinting at something unflattering or damaging, not for gently suggesting good news.
